prompt: After last year's statements were issued, the company finds it forgot to record 10,000 of depreciation for that year (ignore tax). Record the correction this year.

reasoning: A material prior-period error is corrected retrospectively (IAS 8): restate comparatives and adjust opening retained earnings.
It does not go through this year's profit.

why_it_matters: Restatements move equity without touching current profit. Frequent restatements are a strong governance red flag.
common_trap: Debiting this year's depreciation expense, which distorts current profit.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IAS 8: restate comparatives as if the error had never occurred; adjust opening equity of the earliest period presented.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 250: same approach, called a prior-period adjustment / restatement.

prompt: An equity investment the company elected to measure at fair value through OCI rises in value by 5,000 during the year (ignore tax). Record the remeasurement.

reasoning: Under IFRS 9 the FVOCI election for equity instruments sends fair-value changes to OCI.
They never recycle to profit, even on sale.

why_it_matters: Gains in OCI bypass EPS. Look at total comprehensive income to see the full change in shareholders' wealth.
common_trap: Crediting a gain in profit or loss.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IFRS 9: irrevocable FVOCI election for equity investments; gains/losses stay in OCI permanently.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 321: equity investments with readily determinable fair values go through net income; no OCI option.

prompt: Under IFRS 5, which of these qualifies as a discontinued operation?
options: A separate major line of business that has been disposed of or is classified as held for sale
Closing one of 200 similar retail stores
Selling an old delivery van
A product line whose sales fell 30%

reasoning: A discontinued operation is a component representing a separate major line of business or geographical area.
Routine disposals or declines are part of continuing operations.

why_it_matters: Valuation should be based on continuing operations; the split tells you which earnings will recur.
common_trap: Labelling any closure or loss-making product as discontinued.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IFRS 5: separate major line of business or geographical area, disposed of or held for sale.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 205-20: a disposal that represents a strategic shift with a major effect on operations and results.

prompt: A discontinued division lost 300 from operations this year and 200 on disposal. Tax rate 25%. What single amount is reported for discontinued operations?

reasoning: Total pre-tax loss = 500
Net of tax: 500 × 0.75 = 375 loss
Shown as one line after profit from continuing operations

why_it_matters: Discontinued results are net of tax and below continuing profit, so continuing EPS is the base for forecasting.
common_trap: Reporting the losses gross, or within operating profit.

prompt: Net income 1,200,000, preference dividends 200,000, weighted average ordinary shares 500,000. Basic EPS?

reasoning: Earnings available to ordinary shareholders = 1,000,000

why_it_matters: EPS is the denominator of the P/E ratio; small definitional differences move valuations.

prompt: 100,000 shares were outstanding on 1 January and 30,000 more were issued for cash on 1 April. Weighted average shares for the year?

reasoning: New shares outstanding for 9 of 12 months: 30,000 × 9/12 = 22,500

why_it_matters: Weighting matches the shares to the period the new capital was earning.

prompt: Sales 1,000; cost of sales 600; selling expenses 100; administrative expenses 80; finance costs 20; tax 25%. Profit for the year?

reasoning: Gross profit 400; operating profit 220; profit before tax 200
Tax 50; profit 150

why_it_matters: Intermediate subtotals (gross profit, operating profit) are what analysts compare; the bottom line mixes in financing and tax.
common_trap: Taxing operating profit instead of profit before tax.

prompt: Under IFRS, how are material unusual items (e.g. a large restructuring charge) presented?
options: Within profit from continuing operations, disclosed separately (on the face or in the notes); 'extraordinary items' are prohibited
As extraordinary items below net income
Directly in equity
In other comprehensive income

reasoning: IAS 1 prohibits presenting items as extraordinary.
Material items are disclosed separately so users can judge persistence.

why_it_matters: Companies that report 'one-off' charges every year are telling you they are not one-off.
common_trap: Excluding recurring 'non-recurring' charges from valuation earnings.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IAS 1: no extraordinary items; separate disclosure of material items.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: Extraordinary items were eliminated in 2015 (ASU 2015-01); unusual or infrequent items are shown separately within continuing operations.

prompt: A company revises the useful life of its machines from 10 to 8 years. How is this reported?
options: Prospectively, as a change in estimate: depreciate the remaining carrying amount over the revised remaining life
Retrospectively, restating prior years
As a prior-period error
As a change in accounting policy

reasoning: Useful lives are estimates that are revised as information arrives.
Changes in estimate affect the current and future periods only.

why_it_matters: Estimate changes are a quiet way to move profit (longer lives = lower depreciation). Check for them when margins jump.
common_trap: Restating prior years for an estimate change.

prompt: Which combination is the strongest signal of low earnings quality?
options: Profit growth driven by gains on asset sales and lower bad-debt provisions, with flat operating cash flow
Profit growth with matching growth in operating cash flow
A one-off restructuring charge disclosed separately
Higher depreciation after a big capex programme

reasoning: Non-operating gains and provision releases are not repeatable and not cash.
Flat CFO confirms the profit is not converting.

why_it_matters: Valuing low-quality earnings at a full multiple overpays.
common_trap: Focusing on the profit trend without asking where it came from.

prompt: Under IAS 1, how may a company analyse its operating expenses on the face of the income statement?
options: By nature (e.g. raw materials, staff, depreciation) or by function (e.g. cost of sales, distribution, admin), whichever is more reliable and relevant
Only by function
Only by nature
It does not need to analyse them

reasoning: IAS 1 allows either analysis.
If by function, extra disclosure by nature (depreciation, staff costs) is required in the notes.

why_it_matters: By-nature reporting reveals cost structure (materials vs staff); by-function reveals gross margin. You may need the notes to build both.
common_trap: Assuming every company shows a gross profit line.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IAS 1: by nature or by function (IFRS 18 from 2027 adds defined subtotals such as operating profit).
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: SEC registrants present expenses by function; there is no by-nature option on the face.

prompt: A parent owns 80% of a subsidiary that earned 1,000 this year. How is the subsidiary's profit shown in the consolidated income statement?
options: All 1,000 is included; 200 is then attributed to non-controlling interests and 800 to owners of the parent
Only 800 is included
Only dividends received are included
1,000 is included and nothing is attributed to minorities

reasoning: Consolidation includes 100% of the subsidiary's results.
The NCI share is shown as an allocation of profit, not an expense.

why_it_matters: EPS and ROE must use profit attributable to the parent; EV must include NCI to match 100% EBITDA.
common_trap: Using total profit (including NCI) for EPS.

prompt: Other comprehensive income (OCI) items under IFRS

answer.meaning: Gains and losses recognised outside profit or loss.
answer.formula: Never recycled: revaluation surplus (IAS 16/38), pension remeasurements (IAS 19), FVOCI equity investments. Recycled to profit later: FVOCI debt instruments, cash-flow hedges, foreign-currency translation of foreign operations.
answer.high_signals: Large OCI losses: hidden balance-sheet risk (pensions, FX, hedges).

why_it_matters: Big OCI swings change book equity and leverage even when profit looks stable.
common_trap: Assuming all OCI items eventually pass through profit.

answer.meaning: Reconciles opening and closing balances of each equity component.
answer.formula: Opening + total comprehensive income + share issues − dividends − buybacks ± other = closing
answer.interpretation: Shows how much equity came from profit versus owners' transactions.
answer.high_signals: Equity growth from share issues: growth funded externally.
answer.low_signals: Equity shrinking through buybacks and dividends: capital being returned.

why_it_matters: It is the bridge you use to check that a model's equity rolls forward correctly.
common_trap: Forgetting OCI and share-based payments in the roll-forward.

prompt: A company switches its inventory cost formula from weighted average to FIFO because FIFO gives more relevant information. How is this reported?
options: Retrospectively as a change in accounting policy: restate prior periods and adjust opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented
Prospectively from the date of change
As a change in estimate
Only in the notes, with no adjustment

reasoning: Voluntary policy changes are applied retrospectively unless impracticable (IAS 8).
This keeps periods comparable.

why_it_matters: Retrospective restatement means the 'old' year you compare against has changed; use restated comparatives.
common_trap: Treating a policy change like an estimate change.

prompt: Why should an analyst look at total comprehensive income and not only net income?

answer.model_answer: OCI holds real changes in shareholders' wealth that do not pass through profit: pension remeasurements, revaluations, FX translation of foreign subsidiaries, cash-flow hedge results and FVOCI investments. These can be large and recurring (e.g. a company with big foreign operations losing value every year to a weakening currency). Ignoring them overstates performance and hides balance-sheet risk. Look at the trend of OCI, its components, and whether 'recyclable' items will hit future profit.

reasoning: Name the components, explain why they matter, and how to read them.

why_it_matters: Book equity, and therefore ROE and leverage, move with OCI.

prompt: Which is a limitation of the income statement?
options: Some items are measured with estimates and judgement, and some value changes are not recorded at all (e.g. internally generated brands)
It shows cash flows
It cannot show expenses
It is not audited

reasoning: Depreciation, provisions and bad debts are estimates.
Unrecognised items (brand value, R&D outcomes) never appear.

why_it_matters: Two companies with the same economics can report different profits; you have to adjust.
common_trap: Treating reported profit as an objective fact.

prompt: Management's 'adjusted EBITDA' adds back restructuring costs every year for five years, plus share-based payment expense. How do you treat these adjustments?

answer.model_answer: Restructuring that recurs every year is an operating cost of running this business, so I would not add it back (or would normalise it at its average level). Share-based payments are a real cost: employees are paid in shares instead of cash, diluting shareholders; I would deduct it (or count the dilution). So my EBITDA would be below management's. I would reconcile management's figure to IFRS operating profit, check the trend of the adjustments as % of revenue, and value the business on the adjusted-down figure. Persistent large adjustments also lower my confidence in management's reporting.

reasoning: Test each adjustment: is it truly non-recurring and non-economic?

why_it_matters: Inflated adjusted EBITDA drives inflated multiples and covenant headroom.
common_trap: Accepting management's adjusted numbers as the base for valuation.
